```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# Processing to handle moderator analyses
# setting Time 2 strategy perceptions to fill in for Time 1
t1t2Long <- t1t2Long %>% mutate(
  strat_know = case_when(
  is.na(strat_know) == F  ~ strat_know,
  is.na(strat_know) == T ~ dplyr::lead(strat_know, 1)),
  strat_efficacy = case_when(
  is.na(strat_efficacy) == F  ~ strat_efficacy,
  is.na(strat_efficacy) == T ~ dplyr::lead(strat_efficacy, 1)),
  strat_mot = case_when(
  is.na(strat_mot) == F  ~ strat_mot,
  is.na(strat_mot) == T ~ dplyr::lead(strat_mot, 1))
)

# setting Time 1 general perceptions  to fill in for Time 2
t1t2LongKnowledgeT1 <- t1t2Long %>% mutate(
  knowledge = case_when(
  time == 1 ~ knowledge,
  time == 2 ~ dplyr::lag(knowledge, 1))
)
t1t2LongBiasworryT1 <- t1t2Long %>% mutate(
  biasworry = case_when(
  time == 1 ~ biasworry,
  time == 2 ~ dplyr::lag(biasworry, 1))
)
t1t2LongTheoriesT1 <- t1t2Long %>% mutate(
  theories = case_when(
  time == 1 ~ theories,
  time == 2 ~ dplyr::lag(theories, 1))
)

# Formula for computing Cohen's d with the sd of the difference for dependent samples
d_sdDiff <- function(post, pre){
  (mean(post, na.rm=T)-mean(pre, na.rm=T)) / sd(post-pre, na.rm=T)

}

```

```{r baseline characteristics}
# Correlation Matrices
# Function to compute p-values of correlations
# mat : is a matrix of data
# ... : further arguments to pass to the native R cor.test function
cor.mtest <- function(mat, ...) {
    mat <- as.matrix(mat)
    n <- ncol(mat)
    p.mat<- matrix(NA, n, n)
    diag(p.mat) <- 0
    for (i in 1:(n - 1)) {
        for (j in (i + 1):n) {
            tmp <- cor.test(mat[, i], mat[, j], ...)
            p.mat[i, j] <- p.mat[j, i] <- tmp$p.value
        }
    }
  colnames(p.mat) <- rownames(p.mat) <- colnames(mat)
  p.mat
}
# Function to compute df of correlations
# mat : is a matrix of data
# ... : further arguments to pass to the native R cor.test function
cor.dftest <- function(mat, ...) {
    mat <- as.matrix(mat)
    n <- ncol(mat)
    p.mat<- matrix(NA, n, n)
    diag(p.mat) <- 0
    for (i in 1:(n - 1)) {
        for (j in (i + 1):n) {
            tmp <- cor.test(mat[, i], mat[, j], ...)
            p.mat[i, j] <- p.mat[j, i] <- tmp$parameter
        }
    }
  colnames(p.mat) <- rownames(p.mat) <- colnames(mat)
  p.mat
}

# Order: time of measurement
t1t2.corrData <- t1t2 %>% select(
  knowledge.t1,  biasworry.t1, theories.t1,strategy_use, 
  knowledge.t2,  biasworry.t2, theories.t2, strategy_intend,
  strat_know.t2, strat_mot.t2, strat_efficacy.t2
)
graphnames <- c("Knowledge about Bias T1",  "Concern about Bias T1", "Malleability of Bias T1","Strategy Use T1",
                "Knowledge about Bias T2","Concern about Bias T2", "Malleability of Bias T2",  "Strategy Intentions T2", 
                "Feasibility of Strategies T2", "Motivation to Use Strategies T2", "Efficacy of Strategies T2")

# Calculating range of df
table(cor.dftest(t1t2.corrData))

# Creating relevant datasets for visualization
p.mat <- cor.mtest(t1t2.corrData)
t1t2.corrData <- cor(t1t2.corrData, use="pairwise.complete.obs")

colnames(p.mat) <- graphnames
rownames(p.mat) <- graphnames
colnames(t1t2.corrData) <- graphnames
rownames(t1t2.corrData) <- graphnames

# Creating figure
pdf(file = "combined-corrplot_keyoutcomes.pdf", useDingbats = FALSE, width = 9, height = 6.28)
col <- colorRampPalette(c("#BB4444", "#EE9988", "#FFFFFF", "#77AADD", "#4477AA"))
corrplot(t1t2.corrData, method="color", col=col(200),  
         type="upper", order="original", 
         addCoef.col = "black", # Add coefficient of correlation
         tl.col="black", tl.srt=45, #Text label color and rotation
         # Combine with significance
         p.mat = p.mat, sig.level = 0.05, insig='blank',
         # hide correlation coefficient on the principal diagonal
         diag=FALSE 
         )$corrPos -> p1
text(p1$x, p1$y, round(p1$corr, 2)) 
dev.off()
```

### Immediate effects: General perceptions
```{r Immediate effects: General perceptions, echo=F, warning=F, message=F}
lmer.null <- summary(lmer(knowledge ~ (1|id), data = t1t2Long))

# As can be seen in Figure 1, officers were more likely to believe in the existence of subtle or hidden biases after taking the training (b = .69, SE = .02, t = 28.51, p < .001, d = .48). 
anova(lmer(knowledge ~ time + (1|id), data = t1t2Long), lmer.null)
summary(lmer(knowledge ~ time + (1|id), data = t1t2Long))
summary(lmer(knowledge ~ time + (1|id), data = t1t2Long))$coefficients[[6]] # df
d_sdDiff(t1t2$knowledge.t2,t1t2$knowledge.t1)

# After the training, officers expressed more concern about unintended biases relative to baseline (b = .39, SE = .02, t = 17.04, p < .001, d = .28). 
summary(lmer(biasworry ~ time + (1|id), data = t1t2Long))
summary(lmer(biasworry ~ time + (1|id), data = t1t2Long))$coefficients[[6]] # df
d_sdDiff(t1t2$biasworry.t2,t1t2$biasworry.t1)

# We found that the training temporarily reduced beliefs in the malleability of bias (b = -.12, SE = .03, t = -4.45, p < .001, d = -.07), indicating that immediate increases in knowledge and concern about bias were slightly offset by perceptions that bias was less malleable. 
summary(lmer(theories ~ time + (1|id), data = t1t2Long))
summary(lmer(theories ~ time + (1|id), data = t1t2Long))$coefficients[[6]] # df
d_sdDiff(t1t2$theories.t2,t1t2$theories.t1)

```

### Moderators (T1 + T2)

<!-- We examined whether immediate changes in our key outcomes were related to characteristics of police officers. We examined three demographic factors (i.e., race/ethnicity, gender, level of education), two social-psychological individual differences (i.e., police identity centrality, expectations of respect from community members), and three factors about their work experience (i.e., contact with minority groups, rank, and years in department). Characteristics of the officers generally did not predict the amount of learning, with several exceptions that were not robust to changes in model specification. See the supplemental analyses (S4) for a summary of the exceptions. -->

#### Perceptions of respect from citizens (continuous)
**Summary**: Perceptions of respect from citizens did not consistently moderate training effects. (Significant effect(s): 0/4 models).

#### Knowledge of bias (for all key outcomes except themselves) (continuous)
**Summary**: Officers with greater baseline knowledge of bias showed less of a decrease in perceived malleability of bias at Time 2, which may be attributable to lower perceived malleability in bias to begin with. Officers with greater baseline knowledge also showed smaller gains in concerns about bias, which may also be attributable to greater baseline concerns. Overall, these findings indicate  a "leveling" between people who were less knowledgeable and more knowledge about bias at baseline. That would suggest the training is more effective for officers who knew less about bias to begin with.

##### Time 1 to Time 2 (total N = 3764)
<details><summary>Summary tables</summary>
Malleability of Bias
`r knitr::kable(summary(lmer(theories ~ time * knowledge + (1|id), data = t1t2LongKnowledgeT1))$coefficients, digits = c(2, 2, 2, 2, 3))`
Concerns about Bias

Strategy Use / Intentions

\

#### Perceived malleability of bias (for all key outcomes except themselves) (continuous)
**Summary**: Officers who perceived bias to be more malleable at baseline showed larger gains in knowledge, concerns about bias, and intentions to use strategies to mitigate bias at Time 2. However, these effects did not seem to persist through Time 3.

##### Time 1 to Time 2 (total N = 3764)
<details><summary>Summary tables</summary>

\

#### Concern about bias (for all key outcomes except themselves) (continuous)
**Summary**: Officers who were more concerned about bias at baseline showed smaller increases in knowledge of bias at Time 2, which may bias may be attributable to higher  baseline knowledge of bias at Time 1. Officers who were more concerned about bias at baseline also showed larger increases in the perceived malleability of bias at Time 2, which may reflect learning about strategies to mitigate bias.

<!-- We also examined whether immediate changes in our key outcomes were related to characteristics of educators.  -->

```{r follow-up analyses of facilduo_gender}
# Across both cohorts
summary(lmer(knowledge ~ time * facilduo_gender + (1|id), data = t1t2Long, contrasts = list(facilduo_gender=contr.treatment(3, base=3))))

summary(lmer(theories ~ time * facilduo_gender + (1|id), data = t1t2Long, contrasts = list(facilduo_gender=contr.treatment(3, base=3))))

summary(lmer(biasworry ~ time * facilduo_gender + (1|id), data = t1t2Long, contrasts = list(facilduo_gender=contr.treatment(3, base=3))))

summary(lmer(strategy ~ time * facilduo_gender + (1|id), data = t1t2Long, contrasts = list(facilduo_gender=contr.treatment(3, base=3))))


plot_model(lm(knowledge ~ time*facilduo_gender,data=t1t2Long), type="pred", 
           terms=c("time", "facilduo_gender"))
plot_model(lm(biasworry ~ time*facilduo_gender,data=t1t2Long), type="pred", 
           terms=c("time", "facilduo_gender"))

# When the training was in-person, sessions with male-male pairs of educators were linked to lower gains in knowledge about bias than mixed-gender or female-female pairs (bs = .18, .18, SEs = .07, .08, ts = 2.41, 2.18, ps = .016, .030).
summary(lmer(knowledge ~ time * facilduo_gender + (1|id), data = t1t2Long[t1t2Long$cohort==1,], contrasts = list(facilduo_gender=contr.treatment(3, base=3))))

# Male-male pairs also showed lower immediate increases in concern than mixed-gender pairs, (b = .16, SE = .07, t = 2.29, p = .022). 
summary(lmer(biasworry ~ time * facilduo_gender + (1|id), data = t1t2Long[t1t2Long$cohort==1,], contrasts = list(facilduo_gender=contr.treatment(3, base=3))))

# Cohort 2 (online): Characteristics not linked to outcomes
summary(lmer(knowledge ~ time * facilduo_gender + (1|id), data = t1t2Long[t1t2Long$cohort==2,], contrasts = list(facilduo_gender=contr.treatment(3, base=3))))
summary(lmer(biasworry ~ time * facilduo_gender + (1|id), data = t1t2Long[t1t2Long$cohort==2,], contrasts = list(facilduo_gender=contr.treatment(3, base=3))))

```
